passage: On the evening bus through Guwahati, Bhupen had to turn to the window because a street singer's song about the river made his eyes fill. A stranger giving up her seat to an old man could lift his whole day. The same depth cut the other way. When his project partner Lakshmi sent a sharp message about the missed draft, he read it twenty times and couldn't eat dinner. Deadlines sat in his chest like stones. This term he tried something new: two evenings a week marked "river walk" in his planner, no phone, and a rule that he'd reply to hard messages the next morning. When Lakshmi apologised for her tone, he told her, "I feel things loudly. It's not weakness. It's also why I noticed your chart was wrong."

qa.a: "River walk", with no phone.

qa.a: He replies the next morning, giving his strong first feelings time to settle.

qa.a: She may understand her tone hit harder than she meant, and value the careful noticing that caught her chart error.

"You're crying at a bird video again?" Mehak asked, dropping her bag on the hostel bed.
Manjula laughed through her tears. "The mother feeds all four babies. Every single one."
"And yesterday you cried at the sunset."
"It was very orange."
Mehak sat down. "You also didn't sleep after the viva."
"The examiner frowned at slide three. I've replayed that frown a hundred times." Manjula wiped her face. "Everything comes in loud for me, the good and the bad."
"Is that a problem?"
"Only when I don't plan for it. So I've blocked Sunday mornings: no people, just music. And I'm going to stop calling it a weakness."
"Good. Because you're the only one who remembers my mother's birthday."

qa.a: The sunset.

qa.q: What does Manjula replaying the examiner's frown show about how she feels criticism?
qa.a: She feels it very sharply and keeps worrying over it, so one frown kept her awake after the viva.

qa.q: What choice has Manjula made to plan for her strong feelings?
qa.a: She blocked Sunday mornings for music and no people, and decided to stop calling her sensitivity a weakness.

qa.q: How does Mehak see Manjula's sensitivity by the end?
qa.a: As a gift too, since Manjula is the only one who remembers Mehak's mother's birthday.

grounding: A young woman who feels beauty and criticism intensely plans downtime and chooses to see her sensitivity as depth, not weakness.

passage: On the walk home from college in Pune, Akash stopped dead on the pavement. An old man was playing a sarangi outside the bank, and the sound went straight through him; his eyes stung, and he stood there for three songs while Rashmi waited, amused. 'You feel everything, don't you?' she said. He did. The monsoon smell, a stranger's kindness at the bus stop, a good line in a poem. But the same week, when his project group argued over deadlines, the shouting felt as if it were inside his ribs. He couldn't sleep, and lost a whole evening just recovering. That Sunday he tried something new. He blocked two hours in his planner, marked them 'quiet', and spent them by the lake. 'It's not weakness,' he told Rashmi later. 'It's the same wiring. I just need to recharge it.'

qa.a: A sarangi.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when his project group argued?

qa.a: He blocked two quiet hours by the lake; scheduled downtime lets him recover from how intensely he feels.

qa.a: Rashmi is amused and affectionate, noticing that he feels everything deeply.

'Veerji, you're crying at a sunset again?'
Baljeet laughed and wiped his eyes. 'It's pink, Mehak. Look at it.'
'You cried at the wedding band too. And when the chai-wala gave that kid a free biscuit.'
'I know.' He sat on the terrace wall. 'It's wonderful. And it's terrible. That group presentation last week? Arvind snapped at me in front of everyone and I felt it for three days.'
'Three days?'
'Three. Kept replaying it.'
Mehak sat beside him. 'So what, you'll stop feeling things?'
'No. I've started keeping Saturday mornings empty. No plans, no calls. Just walking by the canal.'
'And that works?'
'It helps me come back. The same feeling makes me good at design, Mehak. I just need to refill.'
She bumped his shoulder. 'Okay, sensitive genius. Enjoy your sunset.'

qa.a: Arvind, in front of everyone.

qa.a: He felt hurt for three days, replaying it over and over.

passage: I used to think something was wrong with me. I'm Shalini. The first time I heard a live veena concert, I had to leave the hall because I was crying too hard. A friend's small kindness could keep me warm for a week. But the same thing that made music so huge made my final-year deadlines feel like a wall falling on me. When Ujjwal and I clashed over our thesis chapters, I lay awake three nights. Ujjwal said once, not unkindly, 'You feel everything at volume ten.' It took me a while to stop hearing that as an insult. What changed was small: I started keeping one evening a week empty, and I stopped saving all the hard work for the last two days. I still cry at concerts. I just don't think it's weakness any more. It's depth, and depth needs rest.

qa.q: What made Shalini leave the concert hall?
qa.a: Crying too hard at a live veena concert.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel after clashing with Ujjwal over the thesis chapters?
qa.a: Shalini felt it sharply and anxiously, lying awake three nights.

qa.q: What two changes helped Shalini?
qa.a: Keeping one evening a week empty, and not leaving all the hard work for the last two days.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have meant by 'You feel everything at volume ten'?
qa.a: Ujjwal seems to have been describing Shalini honestly, not unkindly, though at first it sounded like an insult.

grounding: Shows a young adult who experiences music and kindness intensely and conflict and deadlines sharply, and learns to schedule downtime and see sensitivity as depth.

passage:
Mentor's note, second-year music students, end of term.
Gurpreet plays the sarangi like the notes hurt and heal at once. At the college concert, three people in the front row cried. She came off stage glowing.
The same week, a harsh remark from a roommate, Ganga, about the practice noise left her unable to eat. When the theory assignment and two rehearsals fell on the same day, she sat in the corridor with her head on her knees.
I sat beside her. She said, "I feel everything too much. It's a weakness."
I told her what I'd seen at the concert: that the depth people cried at and the sting she felt with Ganga come from the same place.
What I did next: we opened her planner together and she blocked two quiet evenings a week, marked "no plans". I also suggested she and Ganga agree on practice hours. I'll check in after exams.

qa.q: What instrument does Gurpreet play?
qa.a: She plays the sarangi.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel about her own sensitivity when she sat in the corridor?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and ashamed of it, calling feeling everything too much a weakness.

qa.q: What practical steps did the mentor help Gurpreet take?
qa.a: They blocked two quiet evenings a week in her planner, and the mentor suggested she and Ganga agree on practice hours.

qa.q: How might Ganga's remark look different from Ganga's side?
qa.a: Ganga may have just been tired of the noise and not known how hard the words would land; agreeing practice hours could help both of them.

grounding: Shows a mentor watching a young adult who feels music and conflict intensely help her plan downtime and see sensitivity as depth.
